questions.q: Monozygotic twins formed by splitting of the inner cell mass of a blastocyst typically have:
questions.explain: Splitting at the 2-cell or morula stage (days 0–3) gives two chorions and two amnions. Inner cell mass splitting (about days 4–8) gives monochorionic diamniotic twins, the most common monozygotic type. Later splitting gives a shared amnion.

open.q: Monozygotic twins formed by splitting of the inner cell mass of a blastocyst typically have how many chorions and amnions?

questions.q: Dizygotic twins result from:
options: Fertilization of two oocytes by two different sperm
Splitting of one zygote at the 2-cell stage
Splitting of the inner cell mass
questions.explain: Two oocytes are ovulated and fertilized separately. The twins are as genetically alike as ordinary siblings and each has its own chorion and amnion.

open.q: What results in dizygotic twins?
accept: two oocytes fertilized by two sperm

questions.q: What is the most common chromosomal abnormality causing spontaneous abortion (miscarriage) during the first trimester of pregnancy?
questions.explain: Roughly 50% of first-trimester spontaneous abortions carry chromosomal abnormalities; autosomal trisomies account for about half of those, with trisomy 16 being the single most frequent trisomy in miscarriages (never surviving to live birth).

open.q: Which specific autosomal trisomy is the most frequent single chromosomal abnormality identified in first-trimester spontaneous abortions?

questions.q: What is the single most common viable chromosomal aneuploidy in live-born infants, and what meiotic error causes approximately 95% of cases?
options: Trisomy 21 due most often to maternal meiotic nondisjunction
Monosomy X due to a Robertsonian translocation
questions.explain: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is the most common autosomal trisomy compatible with survival to term; ~95% of cases result from meiotic nondisjunction (overwhelmingly maternal meiosis I), ~4% from Robertsonian translocation (such as t(14;21)), and ~1% from postzygotic mitotic mosaicism.

open.q: Which cellular division error accounts for roughly 95% of cases of Down syndrome (trisomy 21)?

questions.q: Which chromosomal abnormality presents in live-born female infants with webbed neck (pterygium colli), cystic hygroma, lymphedema of hands and feet, shield chest, streak gonads, and coarctation of the aorta?
questions.explain: Turner syndrome (45,X) is the only monosomy compatible with postnatal survival in humans, typically resulting from paternal sex chromosome loss during spermatogenesis and presenting with short stature, webbed neck, streak ovaries, and preductal aortic coarctation.

open.q: State the classic karyotype of Turner syndrome.

questions.q: A newborn presents with microcephaly, holoprosencephaly, midline cleft lip and palate, microphthalmia, cutis aplasia of the scalp, and postaxial polydactyly. Which trisomy is most likely?
questions.explain: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) features severe midline developmental field defects including holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, microphthalmia/anophthalmia, polydactyly, and rocker-bottom feet.

open.q: Which autosomal trisomy is classically associated with holoprosencephaly, midline cleft lip/palate, microphthalmia, and polydactyly?

questions.q: Which autosomal trisomy is characterized by prominent occiput, micrognathia, low-set malformed ears, clenched fists with overlapping index and fifth fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and congenital heart defects?
questions.explain: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is the second most common autosomal trisomy at birth and presents with prominent occiput, micrognathia, overlapping fingers (2nd over 3rd, 5th over 4th), rocker-bottom feet, and ventricular septal defects.

open.q: Name the autosomal trisomy characterized by micrognathia, prominent occiput, overlapping fingers, and rocker-bottom feet.

questions.q: During which period of human prenatal development is the conceptus MOST susceptible to the induction of major structural congenital malformations by teratogens?
questions.explain: According to Wilson's principles of teratology, susceptibility depends on developmental stage: insults during weeks 1–2 generally follow an 'all-or-none' rule (embryonic death or full recovery), weeks 3–8 (organogenesis) produce major structural malformations, and weeks 9–38 produce functional deficits or growth restriction.

open.q: Why do teratogenic exposures during the first 2 weeks after fertilization rarely cause surviving infants to have structural birth defects (the 'all-or-none' phenomenon)?
accept: insults either kill the embryo or surviving totipotent blastomeres compensate completely
severe damage causes embryonic death while mild damage is repaired by pluripotent cells

questions.q: What is the conceptual distinction between a 'malformation', a 'deformation', and a 'disruption' in developmental pathology?
options: Intrinsic developmental error; mechanical alteration; destruction of formed tissue
Chromosomal error; single-gene disorder; multifactorial inheritance
Postnatal defect; fetal infection; maternal endocrine disorder
Vascular defect; neural tube defect; failure of organ migration
questions.explain: A malformation results from an intrinsically abnormal developmental process. A deformation is an alteration in the shape or position of a normally formed structure due to mechanical forces. A disruption is the breakdown of tissue that initially developed normally, often from vascular or mechanical injury.

open.q: Distinguish a congenital deformation from a congenital disruption.
accept: deformation is altered shape due to mechanical forces whereas disruption is secondary breakdown of a normally formed structure
deformation results from mechanical molding; disruption results from destruction of previously normal tissue

questions.q: Maternal infection with which viral teratogen during the first trimester produces the classic triad of sensorineural deafness, cataracts, and congenital heart disease (especially patent ductus arteriosus and pulmonary artery stenosis)?
questions.explain: Congenital rubella syndrome (Gregg triad) causes cataracts/microphthalmia, sensorineural hearing loss, and patent ductus arteriosus/pulmonary stenosis, with risk exceeding 80% if maternal infection occurs in the first 8 weeks.

open.q: State the classic clinical triad of congenital rubella syndrome.
accept: cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease
cataracts, deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus

questions.q: What is the most common congenital viral infection in humans, classically presenting with periventricular intracranial calcifications, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, hepatosplenomegaly, and 'blueberry muffin' rash?
questions.explain: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the leading infectious cause of congenital sensorineural deafness and intellectual disability, characteristically causing periventricular calcifications (in contrast to diffuse cortical/basal ganglia calcifications in toxoplasmosis).

open.q: Which congenital TORCH pathogen is the most common infectious cause of congenital sensorineural hearing loss and characteristically produces periventricular brain calcifications?

questions.q: Which protozoan teratogen acquired from cat feces or undercooked meat produces the classic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications?
questions.explain: Congenital toxoplasmosis (Toxoplasma gondii) presents with chorioretinitis, obstructive hydrocephalus, and diffuse parenchymal intracranial calcifications.

open.q: Name the protozoan parasite responsible for congenital chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications.

questions.q: Maternal infection with which mosquito-borne flavivirus during pregnancy causes severe fetal neurotropism resulting in profound microcephaly, cortical thinning, ventriculomegaly, and arthrogryposis?
questions.explain: Zika virus preferentially infects and kills fetal neural progenitor cells, producing congenital Zika syndrome marked by severe microcephaly with overlapping cranial sutures, subcortical calcifications, macular scarring, and congenital contractures.

open.q: Which flavivirus causes congenital infection characterized by severe microcephaly due to destruction of fetal neural progenitor cells?

questions.q: Which congenital spirochetal infection presents with late stigmata including Hutchinson notched incisors, mulberry molars, interstitial keratitis, eighth-nerve deafness, saber shins, and saddle nose?
questions.explain: Treponema pallidum crosses the placenta (especially after week 16); untreated congenital syphilis leads to early rhinitis ('snuffles') and late Hutchinson triad (notched incisors, interstitial keratitis, sensorineural deafness) plus saber shins and saddle nose.

open.q: Name the causative organism of congenital syphilis, which produces Hutchinson teeth, interstitial keratitis, and saddle nose deformity.

questions.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
questions.q: Which sedative-antiemetic drug prescribed in the late 1950s and early 1960s caused severe limb reduction defects such as phocomelia and amelia when taken between days 20 and 36 post-fertilization?
questions.explain: Thalidomide inhibits angiogenesis and cereblon-mediated limb bud signaling during weeks 4–5, causing amelia (complete absence of limbs) or phocomelia (seal-like limbs with hands/feet attached close to the trunk).

open.q: Name the teratogenic drug famous for causing phocomelia and amelia when ingested during weeks 4 to 5 of gestation.

questions.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
questions.q: Which antiepileptic medication taken during the first trimester carries the highest risk of neural tube defects (spina bifida) by interfering with folate metabolism and histone deacetylase activity?
questions.explain: Valproic acid increases the risk of neural tube defects (especially lumbosacral spina bifida) 10- to 20-fold, alongside craniofacial anomalies and cardiac defects; periconceptional folic acid supplementation reduces NTD risk.

open.q: Which anticonvulsant drug is strongly associated with fetal neural tube defects such as spina bifida when taken in early pregnancy?

questions.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
questions.q: Which acne medication (a synthetic vitamin A derivative) is an extreme human teratogen causing microtia/anotia, cleft palate, conotruncal heart defects, and thymic hypoplasia via disruption of neural crest migration?
questions.explain: Isotretinoin disrupts cranial neural crest cell migration and HOX gene expression, causing retinoic acid embryopathy (absent/small ears, micrognathia, cleft palate, conotruncal cardiac defects, and CNS malformations).

open.q: Name the retinoid acne drug that causes severe craniofacial, ear (microtia/anotia), and conotruncal cardiac defects by disrupting cranial neural crest cells.

questions.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
questions.q: Which oral anticoagulant crosses the placenta and causes fetal warfarin syndrome (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses, and optic atrophy) when administered during weeks 6 to 12 of pregnancy?
questions.explain: Warfarin is a small molecule that crosses the placenta and inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase in fetal bone and cartilage, causing nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses; heparin does not cross the placenta because of its large size and negative charge.

open.q: Why is heparin preferred over warfarin for anticoagulation during the first trimester of pregnancy?
accept: heparin does not cross the placenta whereas warfarin crosses the placenta and is teratogenic
heparin cannot cross the placental barrier

questions.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
questions.q: What is the most common preventable non-genetic cause of intellectual disability in the Western world, characterized by smooth philtrum, thin upper lip vermilion, short palpebral fissures, microcephaly, and growth restriction?
options: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (fetal alcohol syndrome)
questions.explain: Prenatal alcohol exposure impairs neural crest migration and neurogenesis, producing fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) with its hallmark facial triad (short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border), pre/postnatal growth deficiency, and CNS dysfunction.

open.q: List the three classic midfacial features of fetal alcohol syndrome.
accept: smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and short palpebral fissures
short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border

questions.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
questions.q: Which class of antihypertensive drugs is strictly contraindicated throughout pregnancy because it causes fetal renal tubular dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, and skull hypocalvaria?
options: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs)
questions.explain: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy because fetal renin–angiotensin system blockade can cause fetal renal dysfunction, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia and related complications, particularly with later-pregnancy exposure.

open.q: Which class of renin-angiotensin system antihypertensives causes fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, and skull hypocalvaria?

questions.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
questions.q: Poorly controlled maternal pregestational diabetes mellitus during organogenesis significantly increases the risk of congenital heart defects, neural tube defects, and which specific rare lower-spine/limb malformation?
questions.explain: Maternal hyperglycemia generates reactive oxygen species that impair caudal mesoderm development, causing caudal regression syndrome (sacral and lumbar vertebral agenesis with lower-limb hypoplasia) as well as transposition of the great arteries and VSD.

open.q: Name the rare developmental anomaly of the lower spine and pelvis strongly associated with poorly controlled maternal diabetes mellitus.

questions.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
questions.q: In utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES), a synthetic nonsteroidal estrogen formerly prescribed to prevent miscarriage, predisposes female offspring to vaginal adenosis and which rare malignancy in young adulthood?
options: Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina or cervix
Granulosa cell tumor of the ovary
questions.explain: Prenatal DES exposure disrupts paramesonephric (Mullerian) duct differentiation, leading to a T-shaped uterine cavity, cervical incompetence, vaginal adenosis, and clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina/cervix.

open.q: Which rare vaginal/cervical malignancy is associated with in utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES)?

questions.q: How do dizygotic (fraternal) twins originate compared with monozygotic (identical) twins?
options: Two separate ova fertilized by two sperm; one zygote that divides into two embryos
One ovum fertilized by two sperm; two ova fertilized by one sperm
One inner cell mass divided after implantation; two separate ova
Two ova fertilized by one sperm; one zygote divided after implantation
questions.explain: Dizygotic twins result from double ovulation and fertilization of two oocytes by two sperm; they share ~50% of genes like ordinary siblings and ALWAYS have dichorionic, diamniotic placentas/membranes (though placentas may fuse secondarily).

open.q: What is the chorionicity and amnionicity of all dizygotic (fraternal) twin pregnancies?

questions.q: If a monozygotic conceptus splits early—at the two-cell to morula stage (days 1 to 3 post-fertilization, before trophoblast differentiation)—what membrane configuration will the twins have?
options: Dichorionic, diamniotic (two placentas/chorions and two amnions)
questions.explain: Splitting before blastocyst formation (days 1–3, ~25–30% of monozygotic twins) yields two separate blastocysts, each forming its own chorion and amnion (dichorionic, diamniotic).

open.q: What chorion and amnion configuration results when a monozygotic embryo splits during days 1 to 3 (morula stage)?

questions.q: Which membrane configuration occurs in the majority (~70–75%) of monozygotic twins when splitting of the inner cell mass takes place at the early blastocyst stage (days 4 to 8 post-fertilization)?
options: Monochorionic diamniotic: one chorion and placenta, with two amniotic sacs
questions.explain: Between days 4 and 8, the outer trophoblast (future chorion) has already differentiated, while the amnion has not yet formed; splitting of the inner cell mass therefore produces two embryos within one shared chorion/placenta but separate amniotic cavities (monochorionic, diamniotic).

open.q: Splitting of the inner cell mass between days 4 and 8 after fertilization produces which type of monozygotic twin placentation?

questions.q: When splitting of the bilaminar embryonic disc occurs between days 8 and 12 post-fertilization (after both the chorion and amniotic cavity have formed), what twin configuration results?
options: Monochorionic monoamniotic: one chorion and one amniotic cavity
questions.explain: Splitting after day 8 (when the amniotic sac has already cavitated above the epiblast) places both embryos inside a single shared chorion and a single shared amnion (monochorionic, monoamniotic, ~1% of MZ twins), carrying high risk of umbilical cord entanglement.

open.q: Which twin membrane arrangement results when embryonic splitting occurs between days 8 and 12 post-fertilization?

questions.q: Incomplete splitting of the embryonic disc after day 13 post-fertilization results in:
questions.explain: If duplication of the primitive streak/embryonic axis occurs after day 13, separation is incomplete, resulting in conjoined twins classified by site of union (e.g., thoracopagus, omphalopagus, craniopagus).

open.q: Incomplete division of the embryonic disc after day 13 results in what type of monozygotic twins?

questions.q: A 27-year-old woman with a monochorionic, diamniotic twin pregnancy undergoes ultrasound at 22 weeks showing one fetus with severe oligohydramnios ('stuck twin') and growth restriction, while the co-twin has severe polyhydramnios, cardiomegaly, and hydrops. What vascular mechanism explains twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS)?
options: Umbilical cord knotting in a shared amniotic sac
Maternal antibodies directed against donor fetal erythrocytes
questions.explain: Monochorionic placentas contain vascular anastomoses. Unbalanced deep artery-to-vein shunts cause chronic hypovolemia, renal hypoperfusion and oligohydramnios in the donor twin, and hypervolemia, polyuria, polyhydramnios and cardiac overload in the recipient twin.

open.q: Which type of placentation is a prerequisite for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS)?

questions.q: Elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) during the second trimester (16–18 weeks) is classically associated with which two major categories of open fetal defects?
options: Open neural-tube defects and open ventral abdominal-wall defects
Single-gene disorders such as cystic fibrosis and sickle-cell disease
questions.explain: Alpha-fetoprotein synthesized by the fetal yolk sac and liver leaks directly into amniotic fluid (and across membranes into maternal blood) when fetal skin continuity is disrupted by open neural tube defects or ventral body wall defects; by contrast, MSAFP is typically low in trisomy 21 and trisomy 18.

open.q: Name two fetal structural anomalies that cause markedly elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) levels.
accept: open neural tube defects and ventral abdominal wall defects

questions.q: What is the key diagnostic difference between chorionic villus sampling (CVS, performed at 10–13 weeks) and amniocentesis (performed at 15–20 weeks)?
options: CVS allows earlier genetic testing but does not provide amniotic-fluid AFP assessment
CVS is performed later and provides fetal lung-maturity testing
Amniocentesis samples placental villi directly for early karyotyping
Amniocentesis cannot provide fetal cells for chromosomal analysis
questions.explain: CVS aspirates placental villous tissue at 10–13 weeks for rapid genetic analysis, whereas amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid and desquamated fetal amniocytes at 15–20 weeks, permitting both chromosomal testing and AFP/acetylcholinesterase measurement.

open.q: Which prenatal diagnostic biochemical marker for open neural tube defects can be measured via amniocentesis but NOT via chorionic villus sampling?

questions.q: Increased fetal nuchal translucency thickness on ultrasound at 11 to 14 weeks gestation is an important first-trimester screening marker for:
options: Chromosomal aneuploidies and some congenital heart defects
questions.explain: Thickened fluid collection behind the fetal neck (nuchal translucency) at 11–14 weeks correlates strongly with trisomies 21, 18, 13, monosomy X (cystic hygroma), and major congenital cardiac malformations.

open.q: What first-trimester ultrasound measurement behind the fetal neck at 11–14 weeks screens for trisomy 21 and congenital heart disease?

questions.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
questions.q: Periconceptional maternal supplementation with which B vitamin (400 mcg/day starting before conception through the first trimester) significantly reduces the incidence of fetal neural tube defects?
questions.explain: Folic acid is essential for purine/thymidylate DNA synthesis and methylation reactions during rapid neuroepithelial proliferation in weeks 3–4; daily supplementation (400 mcg standard, 4 mg if prior affected pregnancy) reduces NTD incidence by up to 70%.

open.q: Name the water-soluble B vitamin taken periconceptionally to prevent neural tube defects.
